# Constraining New Physics Through Neutrino Oscillation Matter Effects

## Introduction

Physics beyond the Standard Model can manifest itself in subtle ways through neutrino oscillation experiments. When new interactions differentiate among the three neutrino flavors, they can produce additional matter effects that modify the standard oscillation patterns. These non-standard matter effects arise because neutrinos of different flavors interact differently with the ambient matter through which they propagate, altering their effective masses and mixing as they travel. Consequently, precision measurements of neutrino oscillations provide a sensitive probe of new physics that would otherwise remain hidden at accessible energy scales.

## Experimental Approach

A promising strategy for constraining the magnitude of these extra matter effects involves a long-baseline neutrino experiment. Specifically, directing the high-energy NuMI beam from Fermilab toward the planned Hyper-Kamiokande detector would provide the necessary baseline and energy configuration to be sensitive to non-standard interactions. The extended propagation distance allows matter effects to accumulate, enhancing the experimental sensitivity to any flavor-dependent deviations from standard oscillation behavior. By comparing the observed oscillation signal with predictions from the standard three-flavor framework, such an experiment could place meaningful bounds on the size of the additional matter effects.

## Dependence on Mixing Parameters

It is important to note that the constraining capability of this approach is not unconditional. In particular, it depends critically on the vacuum value of sin²2θ₂₃ not being too close to unity. When this mixing parameter is maximal (that is, when sin²2θ₂₃ ≈ 1), the sensitivity to the additional matter effects is significantly diminished, as the standard oscillation pattern becomes less able to reveal the presence of new physics. A value of sin²2θ₂₃ that deviates sufficiently from one is therefore essential for the experiment to achieve its full constraining power.

## Implications for New Physics Models

The constraints obtained from such measurements have direct implications for specific theoretical frameworks. In particular, the limits on the magnitude of the extra matter effects can be translated into bounds on the coupling constants and masses of the new particles predicted by models beyond the Standard Model. A prominent example is topcolor assisted technicolor, in which new gauge bosons mediate flavor-dependent interactions. By mapping the experimental sensitivity onto the parameter space of such models, one can determine which regions remain viable and which are excluded, thereby connecting neutrino oscillation measurements to the broader search for new physics.

# Probing Beyond-the-Standard-Model Physics with Long-Baseline Neutrino Oscillations

## Introduction

The study of neutrino oscillations has emerged as one of the most sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). As neutrinos propagate over long distances, their flavor content evolves in a manner governed not only by their intrinsic mass differences and mixing angles but also by their interactions with the medium through which they travel. In ordinary matter, coherent forward scattering off electrons gives rise to the well-known Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein (MSW) effect, an established feature of the SM. However, if new physics introduces additional interactions that distinguish among the three neutrino flavors, these novel couplings would manifest as *extra matter effects*—modifications to the effective potential experienced by neutrinos as they pass through matter. Long-baseline experiments, in which an intense neutrino beam produced at an accelerator facility is directed toward a distant detector, are especially well suited to reveal such deviations, because the accumulated phase differences and matter-induced amplitudes grow with the propagation distance.

## Extra Matter Effects and New Interactions

Any theory that extends the SM by adding new gauge bosons or scalar particles coupling non-universally to leptons can generate flavor-dependent contributions to neutrino propagation. When these new particles mediate interactions that treat, say, the electron, muon, and tau neutrinos differently, they alter the effective Hamiltonian describing oscillations in matter. The result is a shift in the oscillation probabilities relative to the standard three-flavor prediction. By precisely measuring oscillation channels—particularly the appearance and disappearance rates as functions of neutrino energy and baseline—one can search for these anomalous contributions. A non-observation of any deviation places quantitative upper bounds on the strength of the new interactions, while a positive signal would point directly toward specific classes of beyond-SM models.

## The Fermilab-NuMI Beam and Hyper-Kamiokande

This work investigates a concrete experimental configuration: aiming the high-energy component of the Fermilab NuMI (Neutrinos at the Main Injector) beam at the Hyper-Kamiokande detector. The NuMI beamline is capable of delivering an intense, high-energy neutrino flux, while Hyper-Kamiokande offers an enormous fiducial mass and correspondingly large event statistics. The combination of a high-energy beam with a very long baseline enhances the sensitivity to matter effects, because both the standard MSW contribution and any hypothetical extra matter effects scale with the neutrino energy and the propagation length. This configuration therefore provides a favorable setting in which to isolate and constrain new flavor-dependent interactions.

An important caveat is that the sensitivity of this approach depends on the value of the atmospheric mixing angle θ₂₃. If sin²2θ₂₃ lies too close to unity—corresponding to maximal atmospheric mixing—the standard oscillation pattern becomes nearly symmetric between the muon and tau sectors, and the discriminating power for detecting the small perturbations induced by new physics is diminished. Provided, however, that sin²2θ₂₃ is displaced sufficiently from one, the interplay between the standard and anomalous matter effects produces observable signatures that can be exploited to set meaningful limits.

## Translating Constraints into Model Parameters

The oscillation constraints obtained in this analysis are not merely abstract bounds on effective couplings; they can be mapped onto the fundamental parameters of specific ultraviolet-complete theories. In models such as topcolor-assisted technicolor, new massive gauge bosons and additional dynamical states couple to fermions in ways that can produce the very flavor-dependent neutrino interactions probed here. By relating the effective interaction strength to the underlying coupling constants and masses of these new particles, the experimental limits translate into restrictions on the allowed parameter space of the model. In this way, the absence of anomalous matter effects would exclude regions of coupling-mass space, while any detection would indicate preferred values.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these considerations demonstrate that long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments can serve as genuine tests of specific beyond-Standard-Model theories, rather than as generic searches for unspecified new physics. Directing the Fermilab NuMI high-energy beam at Hyper-Kamiokande offers a realistic experimental avenue for constraining extra matter effects, and the resulting limits carry direct implications for the coupling constants and particle masses predicted by models like topcolor-assisted technicolor. This underscores the broader potential of neutrino oscillation measurements to complement collider searches and to probe the structure of new physics at energy scales that may otherwise be difficult to access.

# The New Standard Model

Every industry eventually reaches a moment when its established benchmarks no longer meet the demands of a changing world. When that happens, a **new standard** emerges—one designed to raise expectations, improve performance, and set the direction for years to come.

## Redefining the Baseline

A standard is more than a specification; it is a shared promise of quality and consistency. The **new model** builds on the foundation of everything that came before it while addressing the limitations that experience revealed. By combining proven principles with fresh innovation, it creates a baseline that others will measure themselves against.

## What Makes It "New"

Being new is not simply about being different. A genuinely new model must offer real advantages:

- **Improved efficiency** that reduces waste and saves time.
- **Greater reliability** that users can depend on.
- **Broader compatibility** that adapts to diverse needs.
- **Forward-looking design** that anticipates tomorrow's challenges.

When these qualities come together, the result is not just an upgrade but a shift in how people think about what is possible.

## Setting the Standard for the Future

The purpose of any new standard model is to lead. It establishes a reference point that guides development, informs decisions, and inspires competitors to reach higher. Over time, today's innovation becomes tomorrow's expectation—until the cycle begins again and the next new standard takes its place.

In the end, progress depends on this willingness to reimagine the familiar. The **new standard model** represents that spirit: a commitment to build better, aim higher, and never settle for what once was "good enough."

# Probing Non-Standard Neutrino Interactions with a Fermilab-to-Hyper-Kamiokande Long-Baseline Configuration

## Abstract

Non-standard interactions (NSI) of neutrinos with matter provide a powerful, model-independent framework for probing physics beyond the Standard Model, encompassing effects that could arise from new mediators, extended gauge sectors, or leptoquark exchange. As neutrinos propagate through the Earth, coherent forward scattering encodes these new interactions in matter-induced potentials, making long-baseline oscillation experiments uniquely sensitive to NSI parameters that are otherwise inaccessible.

In this talk, we investigate the sensitivity of a novel long-baseline configuration in which the Fermilab NuMI beam is directed toward the Hyper-Kamiokande detector. The exceptionally long baseline (~2500 km) enhances matter effects relative to existing and planned facilities, offering improved leverage on the diagonal and off-diagonal NSI parameters $\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}$. We present a full three-flavor oscillation analysis incorporating realistic beam fluxes, detector response, and systematic uncertainties, quantifying the achievable constraints on the electron-flavor NSI parameters $\varepsilon_{ee}$, $\varepsilon_{e\mu}$, and $\varepsilon_{e\tau}$.

We demonstrate how the extended baseline helps break degeneracies between standard oscillation parameters—particularly the CP-violating phase $\delta_{CP}$ and the mass ordering—and the NSI couplings, a persistent challenge for shorter-baseline experiments such as DUNE and T2HK. We further explore the interplay between NSI and the precision determination of the atmospheric mixing angle $\theta_{23}$, and discuss the implications of our projected sensitivities for concrete BSM scenarios, including light $Z'$ models and gauged $L_\mu - L_\tau$ symmetries.

Our results indicate that this configuration could provide competitive, and in some parameter regions complementary, constraints on non-standard matter effects, highlighting its potential role in the global program to test the neutrino sector as a window onto new physics.

---

# Draft Opening Paragraph

Neutrino oscillation experiments have transitioned from establishing the phenomenon of flavor mixing to serving as precision probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Beyond the well-established framework of three-flavor oscillations governed by the PMNS matrix, the propagation of neutrinos through matter is sensitive to non-standard interactions (NSI) that can arise from a wide variety of ultraviolet completions. Of particular interest are flavor-dependent interactions mediated by new gauge bosons or composite states, which can modify both the effective matter potential experienced by neutrinos and the source and detection amplitudes measured in oscillation channels. In this work, we examine how the sensitivity of current and next-generation long-baseline experiments to such effects can be leveraged to constrain topcolor-assisted technicolor (TC2) models. These scenarios, which dynamically generate electroweak symmetry breaking and the large top-quark mass through strong topcolor interactions supplemented by technicolor dynamics, generically predict additional $Z'$ bosons and pseudo-Goldstone states with non-universal couplings to fermion generations. We demonstrate that the resulting flavor-violating and flavor-diagonal NSI operators leave characteristic imprints on neutrino oscillation observables, allowing oscillation data to place complementary bounds on the TC2 parameter space that are competitive with, and in some regions surpass, those derived from collider and low-energy precision measurements.

# Research Talk Summary: Beyond Standard Model Effects on Neutrino Oscillations

## Motivation

The study of neutrino oscillations—where neutrinos change flavor as they propagate—has become a powerful probe of physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). The key motivations typically include:

- **Neutrinos require new physics**: The very existence of neutrino oscillations demonstrates that neutrinos have mass, which the original Standard Model does not accommodate. This makes neutrinos a natural window into BSM physics.

- **Matter effects as a sensitive probe**: As neutrinos travel through matter (like the Earth or Sun), they interact with the surrounding particles. Standard matter effects (the MSW effect) arise from Standard Model interactions with electrons. However, **new interactions or new particles** from BSM physics could modify how neutrinos propagate through matter.

- **Precision era of neutrino experiments**: Modern and upcoming experiments (DUNE, Hyper-Kamiokande, etc.) offer the precision needed to detect small deviations from Standard Model predictions.

## Main Point

The central argument of such a talk is typically that **new physics contributions to matter effects** can alter neutrino oscillation patterns in detectable ways. This may include:

1. **Non-Standard Interactions (NSI)**: New forces between neutrinos and matter that modify the effective potential neutrinos experience.

2. **New mediators or particles**: Additional bosons, sterile neutrinos, or dark matter backgrounds that create extra "matter-like" effects.

3. **Observable signatures**: How these effects could shift oscillation probabilities, mimic or obscure standard parameters, and be constrained or discovered by experiments.

The takeaway is usually that **careful measurement of matter effects on oscillations provides a complementary and sensitive test for BSM physics**, potentially revealing new interactions inaccessible to collider experiments.

---

# Abstract

Non-standard interactions (NSI) of neutrinos provide a model-independent framework for parameterizing new physics effects that modify neutrino propagation through matter. In this work, we analyze constraints on neutral-current matter NSI derived from long-baseline oscillation data collected at the NuMI beamline (Fermilab), leveraging the 810 km baseline and matter density profile that enhance sensitivity to the effective NSI parameters ε_αβ. Using a combined analysis of the appearance and disappearance channels, we place bounds on the diagonal and off-diagonal NSI couplings, finding constraints at the level of |ε_ee - ε_μμ| ≲ 0.3 and |ε_eμ|, |ε_eτ| ≲ 0.1 (90% C.L.), while accounting for degeneracies with the standard oscillation parameters θ₂₃ and δ_CP.

We then demonstrate how these phenomenological limits translate into constraints on ultraviolet-complete new physics scenarios, focusing on topcolor-assisted technicolor (TC2). In TC2 models, additional gauge bosons—notably the topcolor Z′ associated with the extended U(1) sector and coloron states—generate effective four-fermion operators coupling neutrinos to first-generation matter fields (u, d quarks and electrons). By matching the low-energy effective Lagrangian to the NSI formalism, we express ε_αβ in terms of the Z′ mass, its mixing angle, and the family-nonuniversal charges characteristic of TC2. The measured oscillation constraints thereby exclude regions of parameter space corresponding to M_{Z′} ≲ 1–3 TeV for representative coupling choices, complementing bounds from collider searches and precision electroweak data.

Our results illustrate that long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments serve as sensitive probes of TeV-scale flavor physics, and that the family-nonuniversal structure inherent to technicolor-class models is directly testable through matter-induced neutrino NSI. We discuss the projected improvement in these constraints from future high-statistics running and the DUNE experiment, which will extend Z′ mass reach and sharpen limits on the associated NSI parameters.

---
